background: Twenty moves are legal from the initial position: two for each of the eight pawns and two for each knight. Four of them, 1.e4, 1.d4, 1.Nf3 and 1.c4, are by far the most popular and the ones worth learning. The rest are rated here so that every first move gets a verdict, but only the good ones are followed further.

1.e4.strategy: Claims a central square at once and opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop, so White can develop quickly and castle early. The price is a pawn that no other pawn defends, so Black can challenge it right away; the game tends to open early and can turn sharp.

1.d4.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn that the queen already defends, so Black has no quick target, and opens the diagonal of the queen's bishop. It also fights for c5 and e5. The game tends to stay closed longer, and the struggle is about space and pawn structure more than early tactics.

1.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece and controls e5 and d4 without committing a pawn, so White can still choose later between a pawn centre, a fianchetto set-up or a quiet build-up. It also rules out ...e5, which would simply lose the pawn. The cost is that White shows little and lets Black make the first big decision.

1.c4.strategy: Fights for d5 from the side and leaves the central pawns at home, so White decides later between building a pawn centre and a fianchetto set-up. Flexible and solid, often with asymmetrical positions when Black takes the centre with a pawn. It develops no piece and does not yet free the king's bishop, so development starts a move later.

1.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, which then watches the long diagonal and supports a later push in the centre. The move commits nothing there, and the game usually becomes a closed, manoeuvring one with that bishop. The risk is that Black takes central space unchallenged.

1.b3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop, which then eyes e5 and presses along the long diagonal on Black's kingside. White lets Black build a pawn centre on purpose and plans to undermine it later; the price is the central space Black gets meanwhile.

1.f4.name: Bird's Opening
1.f4.background: Named after Henry Bird, the English master who first played it in 1855 and kept playing it for forty years; the Hereford Times coined the name in 1885. It is a Dutch Defence with colours reversed.
1.f4.strategy: Controls e5 and prepares an attack on the kingside, at the price of weakening it: the e1–h4 diagonal is open, and the move does nothing for development. The game is unbalanced, a bet that the attack outweighs that risk.

1.Nc3.name: Dunst Opening
1.Nc3.background: Named after Ted A. Dunst (1907–1985), a New York master; in the Netherlands called the Van Geet Opening after Dick van Geet (1932–2012), who played it frequently. Its recorded origin is Blackburne against Noa, London 1883.
1.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece towards the centre and watches d5 and e4 without weakening anything. But it blocks the c-pawn, which White often wants to push, and does not stop Black from taking the centre; ...d5 followed by ...d4 can even chase the knight. Playable, yet a less effective use of the first move than the main ones.

1.b4.name: Sokolsky Opening
1.b4.background: Named after the Soviet player Alexei Sokolsky (1908–1969), whose 1963 monograph defended it. Also called the Polish Opening, and the Orangutan after Tartakower, who claimed that an orangutan at the Bronx Zoo had advised the move before his game against Maróczy at New York 1924.
1.b4.strategy: Gains space on the queenside and prepares Bb2 against e5 and g7. It shows White's plan before Black has shown anything, the pawn on b4 can become a target, and Black simply takes the centre. Rare at the top level.

1.e3.name: Van 't Kruijs Opening
1.e3.background: Named after Maarten van 't Kruijs (1813–1885), who won the sixth Dutch championship in 1878. Nimzowitsch and Larsen played it occasionally; it is the sixth most popular first move, but rare in modern master play.
1.e3.strategy: Opens the king's bishop and keeps every option open, since it can transpose into many openings. On its own it claims little: the e-pawn goes only one step, the queen's bishop stays shut in, and White gives up most of the first-move advantage.

1.d3.name: Mieses Opening
1.d3.background: Named after Jacques Mieses, who used it in his 1910 match against Teichmann. Deep Blue played it against Kasparov in the third game of their 1997 match, which was drawn.
1.d3.strategy: Covers e4 and opens the queen's bishop, a modest claim to the centre. White aims for a flexible set-up with a fianchettoed king's bishop, but it is slow: Black can occupy the centre and take the initiative.

1.c3.name: Saragossa Opening
1.c3.background: Became popular at the Saragossa chess club in 1919; the next year the club member José Juncosa analysed it, and in 1922 a thematic tournament in Mannheim, won by Tarrasch, required the players to open with it.
1.c3.strategy: Prepares d4 backed by a pawn and keeps the structure solid, but it takes c3 from the knight and claims the centre only timidly. Not bad, but the main first moves do more.

1.a3.name: Anderssen's Opening
1.a3.background: Named after Adolf Anderssen, who played it three times against Paul Morphy in their Paris match of December 1858, scoring 1½ out of 3. Steinitz, Blackburne and Mieses tried it later, and Nakamura beat Carlsen with it in an online blitz game in 2023.
1.a3.strategy: A waiting move: it controls b4 and keeps every piece at home, so Black must show a plan first. It does little for development or the centre and hands the first-move advantage to Black, who in effect plays White.

1.h3.name: Clemenz Opening
1.h3.background: Named after Hermann Clemenz (1846–1908), an Estonian player. Among the rarest first moves; Michael Basman has experimented with it as a prelude to 2.g4 or 2.a3.
1.h3.strategy: Takes g4 from Black's pieces and nothing more: it claims no central square, develops nothing, and slightly weakens the kingside where White usually castles. A tempo spent for later, like 1.a3.

1.g4.name: Grob's Attack
1.g4.background: Named after the Swiss master Henri Grob (1904–1974), who analysed it extensively and played hundreds of correspondence games with it; Carl Ahlhausen of Berlin was one of the first to play it, in the 19th century. Michael Basman beat John Nunn with it in 1978. Engines give Black a clear advantage after 1.g4.
1.g4.strategy: Grabs space on the kingside and prepares Bg2 on the long diagonal, hoping for an unprepared opponent. The pawn on g4 is undefended, the kingside is weakened for good, and Black takes the centre. Widely considered one of the worst first moves.

1.f3.name: Barnes Opening
1.f3.background: Named after Thomas Wilson Barnes (1825–1874), the English player who scored eight wins against Paul Morphy in 1858, one of them with 1.e4 f6 as Black. Edmar Mednis argued that 1.f3 is the worst of the twenty first moves.
1.f3.strategy: Covers e4 and nothing else: it develops no piece, opens no line, takes the knight's best square f3 and opens the e1–h4 diagonal against White's uncastled king. Almost any other move serves the same aim better.

1.h4.name: Kádas Opening
1.h4.background: Also called the Desprez Opening, after the French player Marcel Després; Kádas is the name chess sites use today. Among the rarest first moves. David Bronstein liked to tell of a Russian player who always opened with 1.h4 and always won.
1.h4.strategy: Gains space on the kingside and threatens h5 against a fianchetto, but does nothing for the centre or development, and the rook rarely comes out via h3. The side where White usually castles is weakened, and the pawn cannot go back.

1.a4.name: Ware Opening
1.a4.background: Named after Preston Ware, the American player who favoured uncommon openings and played them in tournaments around 1880. Carlsen opened with it against Radjabov at the 2012 World Blitz Championship as a joke, and won.
1.a4.strategy: Attacks b5 and prepares to bring the rook out via a3, but b5 matters to nobody, and after 1...e5 the bishop on f8 keeps the rook in. A lost tempo that ignores the centre entirely.

1.Na3.name: Durkin Opening
1.Na3.background: Named after Robert T. Durkin (1923–2014) of New Jersey, who published his analysis of it in 1959. Also called the Sodium Attack, since Na is the chemical symbol for sodium.
1.Na3.strategy: A knight on the rim controls no central square, and once Black has moved the e-pawn the bishop from f8 can take it and double White's pawns. White gives up most of the first-move advantage; a later c4 or e4 may still reach a reasonable position.

1.Nh3.name: Amar Opening
1.Nh3.background: Named after Charles Amar, a Parisian amateur who played it in the 1930s, probably by Tartakower, who also called it the Paris Opening. Carlsen beat Dreev with it in a 2018 online rapid game.
1.Nh3.strategy: The knight on h3 has little future: it reaches only f4 and g5, and 1...d5 already threatens ...Bxh3, which would double White's pawns on the kingside. Black takes the centre undisturbed.

1.a3 e5.strategy: The natural answer to a waiting move: Black claims the centre at once and opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop. White's pawn on a3 does nothing yet to contest the centre, so Black has a comfortable game and White has to decide how to fight for the squares.

1.a3 a5.strategy: Answers a rim-pawn move with a rim-pawn move, meant to keep White's b-pawn from advancing. It does nothing for the centre or for development, so Black spends a tempo on stopping a plan White may never follow.

1.a4 e5.strategy: The principal answer: Black takes space in the centre, which is exactly what 1.a4 ignores, and opens the diagonal for the f8-bishop. The bishop also stands guard over a3, so White's plan of swinging the rook out along the third rank is shut down for now. Black gets the easier game.

1.a4 b6.strategy: A sound but modest reply: Black prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop on the long diagonal and leaves the centre pawns for later. It is perfectly playable, yet it hands White a free hand to occupy the centre, which 1.a4 has not yet done.

1.a4 a5.strategy: Mirrors White and stops the a-pawn from advancing, which removes any use White might find for the pawn on the edge. It is harmless but passive: Black fails to take the centre that White has left open, and the game starts level in a very quiet form.
1.a4 a5.name: Ware Opening: Symmetric Variation
1.a4 a5.background: With the black pieces, Ware himself played 1...a5.

1.a4 b5.strategy: Gives a pawn away: the b5 pawn is attacked by the a-pawn and not defended, so White simply takes it. Black's only return is an open diagonal for the queen's bishop, which is not enough for a pawn.

1.b4 e5.strategy: Takes a share of the centre at once and opens the diagonal of the f8-bishop toward the b4-pawn, so White has to decide how to treat its flank pawn. The most natural reply: Black stakes a claim in the middle while White has so far only gained queenside space.

1.b4 d5.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn that the bishop on b2 will not hit, and gives up the attack on b4 in exchange. Black gets a classical, comfortable set-up, and White has to show what the early b-pawn move was for.

1.b4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and watches e4 and d5 without committing a pawn, so Black can still choose between a solid centre and a fianchetto of its own. A flexible reply that leaves White's flank play without a clear target.

1.b4 c6.strategy: Prepares to attack the b4-pawn from the flank with the queen or the a-pawn, and keeps the centre pawns flexible. It is a slow, solid reply that asks White to say how the b-pawn is to be kept.

1.b4 e6.strategy: Prepares a solid centre and frees the f8-bishop toward b4 without putting a pawn in the way of the fianchettoed bishop. Taking the b-pawn once White's bishop is on b2 would be a trap for Black: the bishop takes g7 and wins the rook on h8.

1.b4 c5.strategy: A sharp pawn offer that challenges the b-pawn at once. If White takes, Black has given a pawn for pressure on the c5 square and for play against White's loosened queenside; the move pulls the game out of the usual paths at a real price.
1.b4 c5.name: Sokolsky Opening: Birmingham Gambit

1.b4 f5.strategy: Takes control of e4 with the f-pawn and aims for an aggressive set-up on the kingside. The cost is a looser king position, and the bishop on b2 will look down the long diagonal toward g7.
1.b4 f5.name: Sokolsky Opening: Dutch Defence

1.b4 Nc6.strategy: Develops and attacks the b4-pawn, but the knight stands where a pawn advance with b5 drives it away with a gain of time. Black fights for the centre with pieces, at the cost of spending tempi on this one.
1.b4 Nc6.name: Sokolsky Opening: Grigorian Variation

1.b4 Nh6.strategy: A knight on the rim, aimed at f5 and g4, which keeps the e- and f-pawns free. It does nothing for the centre and the knight is awkwardly placed, so White can build up at leisure.
1.b4 Nh6.name: Sokolsky Opening: Karniewski Variation

1.b4 b5.strategy: Mirrors White's move and claims queenside space, but spends a move on a flank pawn while White still has the first word in the centre. The two b-pawns face each other and the game becomes a manoeuvring one in which White keeps the small edge of the first move.
1.b4 b5.name: Sokolsky Opening: Symmetrical Variation

1.d3 e5.strategy: Takes the centre at once, since White's modest first move has left it free. Black gets a full pawn on e5 and easy development, and White has to prove that the flexible, less committal set-up is worth the space it concedes.

1.d3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, which will press on the long diagonal against White's queenside. Black leaves the centre to White for now and relies on solid development and a later counter-strike, a sound set-up against a first move that claims little.

1.d3 c5.strategy: Stakes a claim to the centre from the flank and prepares to meet White's slow set-up with queenside play. Black keeps the choice between a quick ...e5 and a more restrained plan, at the price of a less direct hold on the centre than the e-pawn gives.

1.e3 e5.strategy: Claims a share of the centre at once, and e3 does nothing to prevent it: Black gets space and a free hand to develop. In exchange, White can choose between a quiet, flexible set-up and a direct challenge to the pawn, so Black has to be ready for either.

1.f3 e5.strategy: Takes the centre and opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop, aiming at the e1–h4 diagonal that White's first move has weakened. Black develops with ease while White has spent a tempo on a move that develops nothing and takes the knight's natural square.

1.f3 d5.strategy: Claims a share of the centre with the d-pawn and frees the queen's bishop, a sound reply that gives White no target. It is less pointed than the e-pawn, which aims straight at the weakened diagonal, but Black still has the easier game.

1.f3 f5.strategy: Mirrors White's move and stakes a claim to e4. It is playable, but it fights for the centre only indirectly and opens the e8–h5 diagonal against Black's own king, so Black passes up the simple central development that White's first move allows.

1.f4 d5.strategy: The main reply: Black takes a stake in the centre and controls e4, so White's natural e-pawn advance is not available for free. The game becomes a mirror image of a Dutch set-up, with White's extra tempo against Black's solid structure.

1.f4 Nf6.strategy: A flexible developing move: the knight controls e4, so White cannot easily claim the centre with a pawn there, and Black keeps every set-up open. Most games settle into the same quiet structures as after 1...d5, with Black deciding how to meet White's plan later.

1.f4 f5.strategy: Mirrors White and takes e4 under control with a pawn, but Black opens the e8-h5 diagonal around their own king just as White did. Sound and quiet if White plays patiently, while a central pawn sacrifice can make the game sharp at once.

1.f4 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn to exploit the e1-h4 diagonal that 1.f4 has opened, then goes after the exposed king. Sharp but risky: if White accepts and plays carefully, Black has to pay for the pawn, and White can also sidestep the gambit by transposing to a King's Gambit.

1.f4 h6.strategy: Prepares ...g5 so that the advance is backed by a pawn instead of being a pure sacrifice. But it spends a move on the edge and weakens the kingside, and White builds a broad centre at leisure.

1.f4 Nh6.strategy: An odd-looking knight that eyes g4 and f5, and is safe on the rim because White's d2 pawn blocks the c1-bishop's diagonal. It avoids weakening any pawn and keeps the centre options open, but the knight is far from the action and needs time to find a better square.
1.f4 Nh6.name: Bird's Opening: Horsefly Defence
1.f4 Nh6.background: The move is attributed to Martin Appleberry.

1.f4 b5.strategy: An offbeat flank advance that takes queenside space and prepares the c8-bishop for the long diagonal, where it presses on e4. White can occupy the centre, but then has trouble defending e4 while also going after the advanced b-pawn.
1.f4 b5.name: Bird's Opening: Myers Defence

1.f4 g5.strategy: Throws a pawn forward to open lines against White's kingside, but White simply takes it, or hands it back at the right moment and leaves Black with a loosened kingside and nothing to show for the time spent.
1.f4 g5.name: Bird's Opening: Hobbs Gambit

1.g4 d5.strategy: Takes central space and eyes the g4-pawn with the c8-bishop at once. It is the sound reply: Black makes use of White's loosened kingside and forces White to say what the pawn is worth.

1.g4 e5.strategy: The instinctive centre grab, and a good one: Black builds a pawn centre of his own and can aim at the h4 square, which the g-pawn has left weak. It puts less direct pressure on White than hitting g4 does.

1.g4 g5.strategy: Copies White's move, so neither side has the better-placed kingside pawns. It is safe and keeps the balance, but Black gives up the chance to take the centre and to punish the loosened kingside.

1.g4 f5.strategy: Attacks the g4-pawn at once, but White simply takes it. Black is a pawn down with a loosened kingside and not a single piece developed, so there is little to show for the gambit.
1.g4 f5.name: Grob's Attack: Alessi Gambit

1.h3 e5.strategy: The natural reply: a central pawn that frees the queen and the king's bishop and takes d4 and f4 away from White. White's first move did nothing for the centre or development, so plain developing moves give Black a slight edge.

1.h3 d5.strategy: Takes a share of the centre at once and opens the diagonal for the light-squared bishop, which now eyes the h3 pawn. White's first move has not helped any plan, so Black develops freely with a freer game.

1.h3 h5.strategy: Copies White's slow first move instead of using the free tempo. It does nothing for the centre or development and loosens Black's own kingside pawns, so Black gives away the easy edge that White's waiting move offered.

1.h4 d5.strategy: Stakes a claim to the centre and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal, which makes the rook trip to h3 a blunder at once: the bishop simply takes it. White's flank move has done nothing for the centre, so Black can take space there and enjoy a comfortable game.

1.h4 e5.strategy: Claims the centre and frees the queen and the dark-squared bishop at once. White's h-pawn has done nothing against it, so Black stands comfortably; the pawn on e5 is the target White will challenge first.

1.h4 a5.strategy: Answers a flank move with a flank move. Black spends a tempo on a pawn that does nothing for the centre or for development, so the balance is kept but nothing is gained, and the fight for the centre starts only now. Harmless rather than ambitious.
1.h4 a5.name: Kádas Opening: Koola-Koola Variation

1.h4 c5.strategy: Fights for the d4 square from the wing and keeps the e-pawn free, a sound way to ignore White's odd first move. It does not claim the centre outright, though, and invites White to throw in a wing pawn to deflect the c-pawn.

1.h4 f5.strategy: Controls the e4 square from the flank without occupying the centre. It is sound enough, but it loosens Black's own kingside and the diagonal toward the king, which White can try to use at once.

1.h4 g5.strategy: Offers a wing pawn for nothing: White simply takes it and is a clean pawn up, with the rook on h1 freed. Black's own kingside is loosened and there is no compensation, which makes this an unsound gambit.
1.h4 g5.name: Kádas Opening: Schneider Gambit

1.Na3 e5.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn and frees the f8-bishop at once, since the knight on the rim does nothing about either. Black also gets the threat of ...Bxa3, which would damage White's pawn structure, so White has to spend time on the knight's problems.

1.Na3 g6.strategy: A sound fianchetto that prepares to bring the bishop to g7 and leaves White to show what the knight on a3 is for. It is less direct than occupying the centre with a pawn, so Black gives up some of the early space that White's passive first move offers.

1.Nc3 d5.strategy: The principal reply: Black takes the centre and threatens to push the pawn to d4, which would hit the knight and win space. White's knight is also in the way of its own c-pawn, so White has to decide at once whether to allow that or prevent it.

1.Nc3 c5.strategy: Fights for d4 from the wing and leaves the centre flexible. If White answers with e4, the knight on c3 blocks its own c-pawn and takes some sting out of White's set-up, so Black faces few problems.

1.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: A patient developing move that hands the decision about the centre back to White. Black keeps both a classical central set-up and a fianchetto open, and White has no obvious way to claim a real advantage.

1.Nc3 e5.strategy: Claims the centre at once and invites White to develop with tempo against the e5 pawn. Playable, but it leaves White a slight lasting initiative, and Black has to know the tactical traps that White's knights can set.

1.Nc3 d6.strategy: A modest, flexible move that prepares to meet the centre with ...e5 or a developing knight later. It claims no space now, so White can build a broad pawn centre without being challenged at once.

1.Nc3 f5.strategy: Contests e4 in the manner of a Dutch Defence, but White's knight already watches that square, so the move gains less than against other first moves and loosens Black's kingside. White simply claims the centre with a pawn.

1.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto: Black controls the centre from a distance instead of occupying it. Reasonable, but it leaves White free to take the centre with pawns first, and Black has to prove later that the space is not a burden.

1.Nc3 b5.strategy: Offers the b-pawn for a lead in development, but the knight just takes it, and Black has little to show for the pawn beyond a bishop on the long diagonal. A dubious gambit that gives White an easy extra pawn.
1.Nc3 b5.name: Dunst Opening: Laroche Gambit

1.Nh3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once and punishes the knight's odd square: ...Bxh3 threatens to take it and double White's kingside pawns. Black loses nothing by being the first to occupy the centre, and White has to spend a move on the knight's problem.
